html:
A Roman aqueduct bridge in Constantinople, completed under the emperor Valens in the late 360s or early 370s. It is the best known piece of a water system that brought water from hills in Thrace, and by the 5th century the channels ran for hundreds of kilometres, the longest of the ancient world.

Work began under Constantius II. The stretch that survives today carries the channel across the valley between two of the city's hills, nearly a kilometre long and up to about 29 m high, over what is now Atatürk Boulevard.

Constantinople had no big river, so the water was stored in hundreds of cisterns, such as the Basilica Cistern, to last through sieges and dry summers. The Byzantines and later the Ottomans kept repairing the aqueduct, and it carried water into the city until the 19th century.
